regions.name: Jura
regions.summary: The Jura is a narrow band of vineyards on the western foothills of the Jura mountains in eastern France, facing Burgundy across the Saône plain. Its white grapes are Chardonnay and the local Savagnin; its reds are Poulsard, Trousseau and Pinot Noir. Whites are made in two ways: topped up in cask (ouillé) for freshness, or left under a film of yeast (sous voile) for a nutty, saline style that reaches its height in vin jaune, Savagnin aged for more than six years and sold in the 62 cl clavelin. Four appellations name places, Arbois, Château-Chalon, L'Étoile and Côtes du Jura, and two name styles, Crémant du Jura and Macvin du Jura.

terroir.climate: Continental and cooler than Burgundy, which lies less than 100 kilometres to the west: cold, often snowy winters, warm summers and rain in every season, brought by westerly weather that breaks against the mountains. Spring frost and summer hail are the recurring hazards and can take much of a crop, and the autumn decides the vintage, since Savagnin and Trousseau ripen late. Warmer summers since the turn of the century have made full ripeness more regular.
terroir.soils: Marl is the Jura's signature: the grey and blue marls of the Lias and the coloured marls of the Trias, heavy clays that hold water and stay cool, with Jurassic limestone on the upper slopes and gravel and scree in pockets. The Jurassic period itself takes its name from these mountains. Savagnin is planted on the grey marls, where it keeps the acidity a long ageing needs; Chardonnay does well on marl and limestone alike; Trousseau wants the warmer gravels, Poulsard the marls.
terroir.topography: The vineyards lie on the Revermont, the broken western edge of the Jura plateau, in a strip a few kilometres wide running from near Salins-les-Bains in the north, past Arbois, Poligny and Lons-le-Saunier, to Saint-Amour in the south. Vines face west and south-west over the flat Bresse, on slopes well below the forested heights, and the edge is cut by reculées, deep blind valleys such as the one below Château-Chalon, whose sheltered sides carry steep vineyards.
terroir.water: No great river shapes the vineyard: small streams such as the Cuisance at Arbois and the Seille below Château-Chalon cut the reculées, while the Doubs and the Saône lie out on the plain. The region's water is held in its clay, which keeps the vines supplied in dry summers but makes the soils slow to warm and hard to work after rain.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The most planted grape, made topped up for a taut, Burgundian white or under the veil for a nutty one, and the backbone of Crémant du Jura.

grapes.name: Savagnin
grapes.styles: The Jura's own white, a member of the Traminer family that ripens late and keeps high acidity: the only grape of vin jaune and Château-Chalon, also bottled ouillé or as a younger veil-aged white.

grapes.name: Poulsard
grapes.styles: The most planted red, spelt Ploussard around Pupillin: thin skinned and large berried, it gives pale, perfumed reds of red currant and spice, and is pressed white for crémant and rosé.

grapes.name: Trousseau
grapes.styles: Darker, firmer and later ripening than Poulsard, thriving on the warm gravels of Montigny-lès-Arsures; the same grape as Portugal's Bastardo.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Grown here for centuries, blended with Poulsard and Trousseau or bottled alone, and a part of many Crémant du Jura blends.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: A minor grape admitted to Crémant du Jura and kept out of the still appellation wines.

wines.note: Deep gold, dry and powerful without any fortification: walnut, curry spice, dried apple and a long saline finish. Serve it cool rather than cold, opened ahead, with Comté cheese, morels, chicken in cream or a soup finished with sherry.
A younger veil-aged white from Arbois, L'Étoile or the Côtes du Jura, nutty and tangy but lighter than vin jaune; the bridge for a guest who enjoys fino or manzanilla.
Topped-up whites with no veil character: lemon, white flowers and a chalky tension, closer in spirit to a Mâcon or a Chablis than to vin jaune.
Pale, almost translucent, with red currant, wild strawberry and spice and very light tannin; serve it cool with charcuterie, roast poultry or salmon.
Deeper in colour and firmer than Poulsard, with red cherry, pepper and earth; a match for game birds and mushrooms.
Traditional method sparkling wine, white or rosé, mostly Chardonnay: crisp, fine and dry, a sound alternative to Champagne at a gentler price.
Made from grapes dried for weeks after picking, then aged long in cask: amber and honeyed, with dried apricot, orange peel and quince; a half bottle for blue cheese or fruit tarts.
A mistelle of grape must and Jura marc in white, rosé or red, sweet and strong; poured chilled as an aperitif or with melon and desserts.

made.viticulture: Vines run in small parcels up the marl slopes, trained on wires and pruned to Guyot, the cane often bent into an arch. The heavy clay holds water, so drainage, erosion and rot are constant work, and growers give warm, well drained ground to Trousseau and Savagnin, which ripen last. Spring frost and hail are the main hazards and have cut whole crops sharply in some years. Savagnin meant for vin jaune is picked late, ripe but with its acidity intact. For vin de paille only sound, healthy bunches are picked, laid on straw or racks or hung, and left to dry for at least six weeks before pressing, losing water and concentrating sugar and acid. Organic and biodynamic farming spread early among the small family estates, and the region has long been a centre of wines made with little or no added sulphur.
made.winemaking: Two cellar paths divide Jura whites. Ouillé wines are topped up to keep the casks full, so no veil forms and the wine stays fresh and fruit led. Sous voile wines are left untopped in old casks; as wine evaporates, a film of yeast forms on the surface, shielding the wine from heavy oxidation while giving it the aldehydes and sotolon that smell of walnut and curry. Vin jaune is the long form of this path: Savagnin alone, kept under the veil without topping up for at least sixty months and released no earlier than six years and three months after harvest, in the 62 cl clavelin. Unlike fino Sherry it is never fortified: the veil forms at table wine strength. Reds see short to long macerations and old wood, Poulsard often for weeks with little extraction. Crémant du Jura is made by the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle, and Macvin du Jura by adding aged marc to unfermented must, so the wine never ferments.

law.classification: The Jura holds six wine appellations: Arbois (1936, among the first French AOCs), Château-Chalon (1936), L'Étoile and Côtes du Jura (both 1937), Macvin du Jura (1991) and Crémant du Jura (1995). Arbois and Côtes du Jura cover every colour and style; L'Étoile is for white wines only, vin jaune and vin de paille among them; Château-Chalon is for vin jaune alone, and its growers may decline to make it in a poor year. Vin jaune and vin de paille are not appellations of their own but mentions made under the geographic names, each with its own rules. Côtes du Jura is the regional net, catching wine from the whole vineyard and what the stricter names exclude. Wine made outside the rules, including many natural cuvées, is sold as Vin de France or under the IGP Franche-Comté.

places.name: Arbois
places.note: The northern capital of Jura wine and a commune appellation covering every colour and style around the town where Louis Pasteur (1822 to 1895) grew up and later studied fermentation.

places.name: Pupillin
places.note: A hilltop village above Arbois whose name may follow Arbois on the label; it calls itself the capital of Poulsard, spelt Ploussard here.

places.name: Montigny-lès-Arsures
places.note: A village just north of Arbois whose warm, well drained gravels suit Trousseau, which it claims as its own grape.

places.name: Château-Chalon
places.note: A village perched on a cliff above the Seille, whose appellation is vin jaune alone, from Savagnin on grey marl; Chardonnay or red grown inside the boundary is sold as Côtes du Jura.

places.name: Domblans, Ménétru-le-Vignoble and Nevy-sur-Seille
places.note: With Château-Chalon itself, the four communes the appellation covers, Domblans only in part.

places.name: L'Étoile
places.note: A small appellation just north of Lons-le-Saunier for white wines only, named, by the usual account, for the star-shaped fossil fragments of sea lilies in its marls: Chardonnay and Savagnin, with a little Poulsard pressed white.

places.name: Côtes du Jura
places.note: The regional appellation, running the length of the vineyard from north of Arbois to the south of Lons-le-Saunier, for every colour and style.

places.name: Poligny
places.note: A town in the middle of the vineyard, better known for Comté cheese, whose slopes make Côtes du Jura in every style.

places.name: Arlay
places.note: A village south of Château-Chalon around an old château estate known for vin jaune and vin de paille.

places.name: Sud Revermont
places.note: The southern stretch of the Côtes du Jura around Rotalier and Gevingey, on marl and limestone, where several estates bottle topped-up Chardonnay from named parcels.

producers.name: Domaine du Pélican
producers.why: An Arbois estate founded in 2012 by a Volnay family, bottling topped-up Savagnin beside vin jaune, a clear way to teach the two idioms side by side.

producers.name: Château d'Arlay
producers.why: A historic château estate in the Côtes du Jura, long a reference for vin jaune and vin de paille.

producers.name: Fruitière Vinicole d'Arbois
producers.why: The growers' cooperative of Arbois, an early French wine cooperative, making every Jura style from its members' vines.

producers.name: Henri Maire
producers.why: The large Arbois house that carried Jura wine across France in the twentieth century.

producers.name: Domaine de la Pinte
producers.why: A Pupillin estate farmed biodynamically, known for Poulsard and for Savagnin in the region's different styles.

producers.name: Domaine Labet
producers.why: A family estate in the Sud Revermont known for topped-up Chardonnay and Savagnin from named parcels.

producers.name: Domaine Rolet Père et Fils
producers.why: An Arbois family estate making the full range of Jura styles, from Poulsard and Trousseau to vin jaune.

exam: Name the five grapes of the still appellation wines: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard, Trousseau and Pinot Noir.
Know vin jaune cold: Savagnin only, at least sixty months untopped under the veil, released after six years and three months, in the 62 cl clavelin.
Separate ouillé, topped up and fresh, from sous voile, untopped, nutty and saline.
Place the four geographic appellations and what each allows: Arbois everything, L'Étoile whites only, Château-Chalon vin jaune only, Côtes du Jura the regional net.
Know vin de paille as a dried-grape sweet wine and Macvin du Jura as a mistelle of must and marc.
Tie Pupillin to Poulsard and Montigny-lès-Arsures to Trousseau.
Relate the marl and limestone to the Jurassic period, which takes its name from these mountains.
traps: Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc: it belongs to the Traminer family, kin to Gewürztraminer.
Vin jaune is never fortified, unlike fino Sherry, though both age under a film of yeast.
Château-Chalon is an appellation, not a château, and makes vin jaune only.
Vin de paille is dried-grape wine: neither botrytised nor fortified.
Macvin du Jura is a mistelle, marc added before any fermentation, not a vin doux naturel.
Poulsard's pale colour does not make it a rosé: it is made and sold as a red.
Trousseau is the same grape as Portugal's Bastardo.

cards.f: The Jura's five grapes for still appellation wine
cards.b: White: Chardonnay and Savagnin. Red: Poulsard (Ploussard), Trousseau and Pinot Noir.

cards.f: Château-Chalon: what the appellation allows
cards.b: Vin jaune only, from Savagnin; anything else grown inside its boundary is sold as Côtes du Jura.

cards.f: L'Étoile: its wines and its name
cards.b: White wines only, still, vin jaune and vin de paille; named, by the usual account, for the star-shaped fossil fragments of sea lilies in its marls.

cards.f: Vin de paille: how it is made
cards.b: Healthy bunches dried on straw or racks, or hung, for at least six weeks, then pressed and aged; sold no earlier than three years after harvest, usually in half bottles.

cards.f: Macvin du Jura: what it is
cards.b: A mistelle: unfermented Jura grape must stopped with Jura marc before any fermentation, in white, rosé and red; AOC since 1991.

questions.q: Which grape is the only one permitted in vin jaune?
questions.exp: Vin jaune is Savagnin alone, a late ripening Traminer that keeps the acidity a long ageing needs. Sauvignon Blanc is a different grape despite the similar name, and Chardonnay goes into other Jura whites.

questions.q: What is the name of the 62 cl bottle reserved for vin jaune?
questions.exp: The clavelin is said to hold what remains of a litre after the years of evaporation under the veil, and the law keeps the shape for vin jaune.

questions.q: Which Jura appellation may be used for vin jaune only?
questions.exp: Château-Chalon admits vin jaune alone. L'Étoile allows white wines of every kind, the Côtes du Jura covers every colour and style, and Crémant du Jura is sparkling wine only.

questions.q: How long after its harvest must vin jaune wait before it may be released?
questions.exp: Vin jaune waits six years and three months from harvest, at least sixty months of it under the veil without topping up.

questions.q: What forms on the surface of an untopped cask of Savagnin as it becomes vin jaune?
questions.exp: As wine evaporates from the untopped cask a film of yeast, the voile, grows on the surface, shielding the wine and giving its walnut and curry notes.

questions.q: Which pale, thin-skinned red is the most planted red grape of the Jura?
questions.exp: Poulsard, spelt Ploussard around Pupillin, gives pale, perfumed reds. Trousseau is darker and firmer, Pinot Noir is grown less, and Mondeuse Noire belongs to Savoie.

questions.q: Under which name is the Jura's Trousseau grown in Portugal?
questions.exp: Trousseau and Portugal's Bastardo are the same grape, used in the Douro for Port and red blends; Galicia knows it as Merenzao.

questions.q: Which commune lies inside the Château-Chalon appellation?
questions.exp: Château-Chalon covers four communes: Château-Chalon, Domblans in part, Ménétru-le-Vignoble and Nevy-sur-Seille. Pupillin and Montigny-lès-Arsures are Arbois villages; Rotalier lies in the southern Côtes du Jura.

regions.name: Savoie and Bugey
regions.summary: Savoie is France's alpine vineyard, a scatter of slopes in the departments of Savoie and Haute-Savoie between Lake Geneva and the Isère valley, with Bugey across the Rhône in the Ain. Its wines are light, fresh and mostly white: Jacquère for the everyday carafe, Altesse for Roussette de Savoie, Roussanne under its local name Bergeron at Chignin, and Chasselas by Lake Geneva. Mondeuse Noire gives a dark, peppery red. The regional appellation, Vin de Savoie or simply Savoie, may add one of sixteen crus to its name; Roussette de Savoie, Seyssel and Crémant de Savoie complete the list, and Bugey has its own appellations, with the sweet, pink, sparkling Cerdon.

terroir.climate: Continental with an alpine edge: cold winters, warm summers and generous rain, softened around Lake Geneva and the Lac du Bourget, whose water stores heat and tempers frost, and by the warm, dry föhn wind that blows down the valleys in spring and autumn. South-facing slopes catch the sun while nights stay cool, so the wines keep bright acidity and modest alcohol; altitude and a wide gap between day and night temperatures shape the style.
terroir.soils: Limestone in many forms: scree fallen from the cliffs, as at Apremont and Abymes on the rubble of the Mont Granier landslide of 1248; glacial moraine and gravel left by the retreating ice, above all around Lake Geneva; marl and molasse on the lower slopes; and schist in the high valleys of the Tarentaise and Maurienne. These stony, free-draining soils warm quickly, a help to ripening in a cool climate.
terroir.topography: No single slope but many pockets at the foot of the mountains, on slopes facing south and south-east above the valley floors. The main stretch is the Combe de Savoie, the broad glacial valley of the Isère north-east of Chambéry, where vines climb the right bank under the Bauges massif. Others sit above the Lac du Bourget, along the upper Rhône at Seyssel and Chautagne, in the Arve valley below Mont Blanc and on the gravel terraces by Lake Geneva.
terroir.water: Lake Geneva and the Lac du Bourget temper the climate of the vineyards around them, reflecting light and storing warmth. The Rhône, the Isère and the Arve carve the valleys that hold the vines, and the Rhône divides Savoie from Bugey.

grapes.name: Jacquère
grapes.styles: The most planted grape: light, crisp and low in alcohol, with white flowers, pear and a flinty freshness; the grape of Apremont and Abymes.

grapes.name: Altesse
grapes.styles: Also called Roussette, the only grape of Roussette de Savoie: fuller and more aromatic, with quince, bergamot and almond, and the acidity to age.

grapes.name: Mondeuse Noire
grapes.styles: Savoie's signature red: deep purple, peppery and violet scented, with lively acid and real tannin, and a serious red at Arbin.

grapes.name: Roussanne
grapes.styles: Called Bergeron here and the only grape of Chignin-Bergeron: rich, with apricot and honey, grown on limestone scree.

grapes.name: Chasselas
grapes.styles: The white of Lake Geneva's crus: delicate, low in acid, often with a faint prickle.

grapes.name: Gamay
grapes.styles: A common light red of Savoie and Bugey, and with Poulsard the grape of Bugey Cerdon.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Light, fresh reds in Savoie and in Bugey, where it grows beside Gamay and Mondeuse.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The leading white of Bugey and a permitted partner in Crémant de Savoie.

grapes.name: Gringet
grapes.styles: A rare white grown essentially at Ayze in the Arve valley, made still and sparkling.

grapes.name: Persan
grapes.styles: An old red of Savoie, nearly lost and now replanted: deep coloured, tannic and fresh.

wines.note: Pale, light and crisp Jacquère, low in alcohol, with green apple, white flowers and a flinty finish; the carafe for fondue, raclette and lake fish.
Fuller and rounder, with quince, bergamot and almond, and the acidity to age a few years; with Beaufort cheese, freshwater fish in butter or poultry in cream.
Roussanne on scree: ripe apricot, honey and a mineral line, rich yet fresh; with veal, pork or richer fish.
Delicate, dry Chasselas from Lake Geneva, sometimes with a light prickle, smelling of white flowers and almond; a lakeside aperitif and a match for perch.
Deep purple, with black cherry, violet and white pepper, bright acidity and firm tannin; with the local diot sausages, game and mountain cheeses.
Traditional method sparkling wine built mostly on Jacquère and Altesse: crisp, light, citrus and floral, an easy aperitif.
Pink, gently sparkling and sweet, low in alcohol, from Gamay and Poulsard; serve it cold with fruit desserts or on its own.

made.viticulture: Vineyards are small and scattered, often on steep slopes where much of the work is done by hand. Growers chase sun and drainage: slopes facing south and south-east, stony scree and moraine, and the warmth thrown back by the lakes. Frost in the valley bottoms and summer hail are the hazards, while the föhn helps ripen the grapes in autumn. Jacquère crops generously and is picked for freshness; Altesse, Roussanne and Mondeuse need warm sites to ripen fully. Warmer summers have made Mondeuse riper and more regular, and old local grapes such as Persan, Gringet and Mondeuse Blanche have been saved by a few growers and replanted.
made.winemaking: The style is fresh and direct. Jacquère and Chasselas are fermented cool in stainless steel or old wood, often kept on their lees and bottled early, sometimes holding a trace of carbon dioxide for liveliness. Altesse and Bergeron may see longer lees ageing or some oak and are made to age a few years. Mondeuse is handled like a northern Rhône red, with moderate extraction and ageing in old casks to keep its pepper and fruit. Crémant de Savoie is made by the traditional method, with the local Jacquère and Altesse making up at least 60 per cent of the blend, and Seyssel has its own traditional method sparkling wine. Bugey Cerdon is made by the ancestral method: fermentation begins in tank and finishes in bottle, where it is stopped while sugar remains, leaving a sweet, lightly alcoholic pink wine with no added liqueur.

law.classification: Savoie has four appellations. The regional AOC, written Vin de Savoie or simply Savoie, covers white, red, rosé and sparkling wine, and sixteen crus may add their names to it, each with its own grapes: Apremont and Abymes for Jacquère, Chignin-Bergeron for Roussanne, Arbin and Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte for Mondeuse, and Crépy, Marin, Marignan and Ripaille for Chasselas among them. Roussette de Savoie is Altesse alone and has four crus of its own. Seyssel (1942), on both banks of the Rhône, makes still and sparkling whites, and Crémant de Savoie, created in 2014, is the traditional method sparkling wine of the whole region. Across the Rhône, Bugey and Roussette du Bugey rose from VDQS to AOC in 2009, with the crus Cerdon, Manicle and Montagnieu. Wine from outside these rules may be sold as IGP Vin des Allobroges.

places.name: Lake Geneva
places.note: The vineyards on the French shore of the lake, in the Chablais near Thonon-les-Bains, where Chasselas makes the crus Crépy, Marin, Marignan and Ripaille on gravel and moraine.

places.name: Ripaille
places.note: A cru around the château of Ripaille on the lakeshore by Thonon, given over to Chasselas.

places.name: Crépy, Marin and Marignan
places.note: The other Chasselas crus of the lakeshore, delicate dry whites on glacial gravels.

places.name: Ayze
places.note: A cru in the Arve valley below the Mont Blanc massif, where the rare Gringet makes still and sparkling whites.

places.name: Seyssel
places.note: Two towns of the same name facing each other across the Rhône, one in the Ain and one in Haute-Savoie, an appellation since 1942 for still Altesse whites and a traditional method sparkling wine that keeps the local Molette.

places.name: Frangy
places.note: A Roussette de Savoie cru near Seyssel in Haute-Savoie, for Altesse.

places.name: Chautagne
places.note: A Vin de Savoie cru between the Rhône and the north end of the Lac du Bourget, known for light reds as well as whites.

places.name: Jongieux
places.note: A cru on the slopes above the Rhône west of the Lac du Bourget, for Jacquère, Gamay, Mondeuse and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Marestel
places.note: A steep limestone slope above Jongieux, a Roussette de Savoie cru known for long-lived Altesse.

places.name: Monthoux and Monterminod
places.note: The other two Roussette de Savoie crus, small slopes near the Lac du Bourget and Chambéry.

places.name: Apremont and Abymes
places.note: Two Jacquère crus south of Chambéry on the rubble of the Mont Granier, whose face collapsed in November 1248; the broken limestone drains fast and warms quickly.

places.name: Combe de Savoie
places.note: The broad Isère valley north-east of Chambéry, where the vines face south-east under the Bauges massif: the main stretch of the Savoie vineyard.

places.name: Chignin
places.note: A cru at the head of the Combe, for Jacquère whites and some red as Chignin and for Roussanne alone as Chignin-Bergeron, on limestone scree.

places.name: Arbin
places.note: The cru for Mondeuse Noire, dark and peppery red on warm south-east facing slopes.

places.name: Cruet, Montmélian, Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte and Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré
places.note: Further crus of the Combe and the slopes near Chambéry, for Jacquère and, at Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte, for Mondeuse.

places.name: Tarentaise and Maurienne
places.note: The high valleys of the Isère and the Arc, where a few estates have revived vineyards on schist with Persan, Mondeuse and Jacquère, sold mostly as IGP Vin des Allobroges.

places.name: Bugey
places.note: Across the Rhône in the Ain, between Savoie and the Jura: Chardonnay, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Mondeuse and Altesse under the appellations Bugey and Roussette du Bugey, both AOC since 2009.

places.name: Cerdon
places.note: The Bugey cru for a sweet, pink, lightly sparkling wine of Gamay and Poulsard made by the ancestral method.

places.name: Montagnieu
places.note: A cru in the south of Bugey for traditional method sparkling wine and for Roussette du Bugey.

places.name: Manicle and Virieu-le-Grand
places.note: Bugey's two smaller crus, Manicle for still Bugey and Virieu-le-Grand for Roussette du Bugey.

producers.name: Château de Ripaille
producers.why: The historic château on Lake Geneva near Thonon-les-Bains whose vineyard gives the Chasselas cru of Ripaille its name.

producers.name: Domaine Belluard
producers.why: The Ayze estate whose still and sparkling Gringet made it the reference for this rare grape.

producers.name: Domaine des Ardoisières
producers.why: An estate that brought vines back to the schist terraces of the Tarentaise, bottling its wines as IGP Vin des Allobroges.

producers.name: Prieuré Saint-Christophe
producers.why: An estate at Fréterive in the Combe de Savoie whose long-aged Mondeuse showed the grape can make a serious red.

producers.name: Domaine Dupasquier
producers.why: A family estate at Jongieux known for long-lived Roussette de Savoie Marestel.

producers.name: Domaine Renardat-Fâche
producers.why: A family estate in Bugey known for Cerdon made by the ancestral method.

exam: Name the grape behind each label: Jacquère in Apremont and Abymes, Altesse in Roussette, Roussanne in Chignin-Bergeron, Mondeuse Noire in Arbin, Chasselas by Lake Geneva.
Know that the regional AOC, Vin de Savoie or Savoie, carries sixteen crus, and Roussette de Savoie four.
Place Seyssel on both banks of the Rhône and know its still Altesse and its sparkling wine.
Know Crémant de Savoie as the traditional method wine created in 2014, at least 60 per cent Jacquère and Altesse.
Describe Bugey Cerdon: pink, sweet, lightly sparkling, Gamay and Poulsard, by the ancestral method.
Link the style to altitude, the lakes and the föhn: fresh, light wines of modest alcohol.
traps: Roussette is Altesse; Bergeron is Roussanne: two similar words, two grapes.
Chignin alone is chiefly a Jacquère white, though it makes some red; Chignin-Bergeron is Roussanne alone.
Mondeuse Noire is not Syrah, though Mondeuse Blanche is one of Syrah's parents.
Cerdon is made by the ancestral method, not the traditional method, and it is sweet.
Bugey lies in the Ain, not in Savoie, and has appellations of its own.
Chasselas belongs to the Lake Geneva crus, not to the Combe de Savoie.

cards.f: Jacquère: where and what
cards.b: Savoie's most planted grape: a light, crisp white low in alcohol; the grape of Apremont and Abymes.

cards.f: Roussette de Savoie: the grape
cards.b: Altesse alone, Roussette being its local name: fuller, with quince and bergamot, and able to age.

cards.f: Chignin-Bergeron: the grape
cards.b: Roussanne, called Bergeron in Savoie. Chignin without Bergeron is chiefly Jacquère white, with some red.

cards.f: Mondeuse Noire: style and stronghold
cards.b: A dark, peppery, violet-scented red with bright acid and real tannin; Arbin is its cru.

cards.f: Vin de Savoie: how many crus
cards.b: Sixteen, each added after the name with its own grapes; the regional AOC may also be written simply Savoie.

cards.f: Bugey Cerdon: style and method
cards.b: Pink, sweet, lightly sparkling and low in alcohol, from Gamay and Poulsard, made by the ancestral method.

cards.f: Apremont and Abymes: the landslide
cards.b: Both crus grow on the limestone rubble of the Mont Granier, whose face collapsed in November 1248.

cards.f: Seyssel: where and what
cards.b: On both banks of the Rhône, in the Ain and Haute-Savoie; AOC since 1942 for still Altesse whites and a traditional method sparkling wine with Molette.

cards.f: Ayze: its grape and its wines
cards.b: Gringet, a rare local white, made still and sparkling in the Arve valley.

cards.f: Roussette de Savoie: its four crus
cards.b: Frangy, Marestel, Monterminod and Monthoux.

questions.q: Which grape makes Roussette de Savoie?
questions.exp: Roussette is the local name of Altesse, the only grape of the appellation. Roussanne goes into Chignin-Bergeron, Jacquère into Apremont and Abymes, Chasselas into the Lake Geneva crus.

questions.q: Which grape is grown for the Savoie cru Chignin-Bergeron?
questions.exp: Bergeron is Savoie's name for Roussanne, and Chignin-Bergeron is Roussanne alone. Altesse is the grape of Roussette, Marsanne is Roussanne's partner in the Rhône, and Mondeuse Blanche is an old Savoie white; none has a place in the cru.

questions.q: Which red grape gives Arbin its dark, peppery wines?
questions.exp: Arbin is the cru for Mondeuse Noire, Savoie's structured red of black cherry, violet and pepper.

questions.q: By which method is Bugey Cerdon made?
questions.exp: Cerdon is a single fermentation finished in bottle and stopped while sugar remains, so it is sweet, pink and low in alcohol, with no second fermentation and no added liqueur.

questions.q: How many crus may add their names to the regional AOC Vin de Savoie?
questions.exp: Sixteen crus follow the regional name, each with its own grapes. Four is the number of crus of Roussette de Savoie.

questions.q: What minimum share of the blend must Jacquère and Altesse make up in Crémant de Savoie?
questions.exp: Crémant de Savoie must hold at least 60 per cent of the local Jacquère and Altesse, with Chardonnay among the permitted partners.

questions.q: Which rare white grape is the speciality of the cru Ayze in the Arve valley?
questions.exp: Gringet grows essentially only at Ayze, where it makes still and sparkling whites; it is not Savoie's common white, Jacquère.

questions.q: Which is one of the four crus of Roussette de Savoie?
questions.exp: Marestel, on steep limestone above Jongieux, is a Roussette de Savoie cru with Frangy, Monterminod and Monthoux. Chautagne, Jongieux and Cruet are crus of Vin de Savoie.

regions.name: South West France
regions.summary: South West France, the Sud-Ouest, is the wine country between Bordeaux and the Languedoc, running from the Dordogne south to the Pyrenees and the Spanish border. It is a patchwork of small appellations and old local grapes rather than one region. Five names carry the exam: Bergerac, Bordeaux's grapes on the Dordogne; Monbazillac, its botrytised sweet white; Cahors, dark red from at least 70 per cent Malbec, called Côt here; Madiran, firm red led by Tannat; and Jurançon, Gros and Petit Manseng in the Pyrenean foothills, dry as Jurançon Sec and sweet from grapes shrivelled on the vine. Gascony's IGP whites and Gaillac's local grapes complete the picture.

terroir.climate: The Court files the South West and the Dordogne as continental, and away from the coast the seasons are marked: warm to hot summers, cold winters and spring frost. The Atlantic still reaches inland, bringing rain and mild, damp autumns to Bergerac, Gascony and the Pyrenean foothills, where both noble rot and mildew follow. Near Toulouse the warm south-easterly autan wind gives Gaillac and Fronton a Mediterranean edge, and in Jurançon the foehn, a warm, dry wind off the Pyrenees, lets late grapes shrivel on the vine.
terroir.soils: Each appellation has its own ground. Cahors divides between the Lot valley's terraces of gravel, sand and clay and the limestone causse above them, patched with red, iron-rich clay. Madiran and Saint-Mont lie on clay, clay-limestone and pebbly clay; Jurançon on clay, sandstone and a coarse pebble conglomerate, the poudingue. Bergerac's slopes are limestone and clay-limestone above the Dordogne's sand and gravel. Fronton grows on the Tarn's old, iron-rich terraces, Marcillac on red clay and sandstone, the rougier.
terroir.topography: An inland country of river valleys and rolling hills, landlocked in the Court's words, framed by the Massif Central to the east and the Pyrenees to the south. Bergerac and Duras continue the Bordeaux slopes upstream; Cahors lies in the deep meanders of the Lot; Gaillac and Fronton sit on the Tarn's terraces near Toulouse. Southward the land climbs through the Gascon hills to the Pyrenean foothills, where Jurançon's vines face south on steep slopes and Irouléguy's climb terraces in the Basque hills near Spain.
terroir.water: Rivers made the region and its history. The Dordogne flows west from the Massif Central through Bergerac; the Lot winds through Cahors; the Tarn crosses Gaillac and Fronton before joining the Garonne, which carried them all to Bordeaux; the Adour drains Madiran, Saint-Mont and Tursan. For centuries the wines of this high country waited at Bordeaux until the city had sold its own, a privilege ended in 1776.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Called Côt or Auxerrois here: at least 70 per cent of Cahors, giving dark, firm, savoury reds of plum, black cherry and earth, and a partner in Bergerac and Buzet.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.styles: The grape of Madiran and Irouléguy and a part of Saint-Mont and Béarn: deep colour, powerful tannin, black fruit and spice, softened by time, oak or micro-oxygenation.

grapes.name: Petit Manseng
grapes.styles: Small, thick-skinned berries that hang into late autumn and shrivel on the vine while keeping high acidity: the heart of sweet Jurançon and Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh.

grapes.name: Gros Manseng
grapes.styles: Larger berried and more productive: the base of Jurançon Sec and a crisp, tropical white of the Côtes de Gascogne.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: With the two Cabernets the core of Bergerac, Buzet and Côtes de Duras reds, and a softening partner in Cahors.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Called Bouchy in Madiran and Axeria in Irouléguy, and a Bordeaux partner in the reds of Bergerac.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A partner in Bergerac, Buzet, Madiran and Irouléguy, giving structure where it ripens on warm ground.

grapes.name: Sémillon
grapes.styles: The main grape of Monbazillac and Saussignac, where noble rot concentrates it, and of the rounder dry Bergerac whites.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Gives Bergerac Sec its freshness, beside Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle, and lifts the sweet wines of Monbazillac.

grapes.name: Muscadelle
grapes.styles: A floral partner in the whites of Bergerac and in Monbazillac.

grapes.name: Colombard
grapes.styles: With Ugni Blanc the old brandy grape of Armagnac, now the crisp, fruity base of Côtes de Gascogne white.

grapes.name: Fer Servadou
grapes.styles: Mansois in Marcillac, Braucol in Gaillac and Pinenc in Madiran: a red-berried, peppery and fresh red grape.

grapes.name: Négrette
grapes.styles: Fronton's own red grape: soft, fruity and scented with violets, for reds and rosés drunk young.

grapes.name: Mauzac
grapes.styles: Gaillac's white for still, sweet and sparkling wine, with a flavour of apple skin.

grapes.name: Len de l'El
grapes.styles: Gaillac's other white, its Occitan name meaning far from the eye, after its long-stalked bunches.

wines.note: Dark, firm and savoury: black plum, black cherry, violet and an earthy, iron grip, drier and more tannic than a Mendoza Malbec. Decant a young one and serve it with duck breast, cassoulet, lamb or Périgord truffle.
Deep and tannic, with black fruit, liquorice and spice, built for years in bottle. Give it air and rich food: duck confit, cassoulet, rack of lamb or foie gras.
Dry and vivid from Gros Manseng: grapefruit, pineapple and white flowers over high acidity, for river fish and Bayonne ham.

Sweet wine from grapes shrivelled on the vine, Petit Manseng above all: candied pineapple, mango, honey and spice, with a fresh acid line that keeps it from cloying. Pour it with foie gras, blue cheese or fruit tarts.

Botrytised sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle: apricot, honey and marmalade, a little lighter than Sauternes. Serve it with foie gras or savoury dishes in a sweet sauce, desserts of peach, apricot, pear, apple, citrus or caramel, and salty or creamy cheeses.
Merlot and the Cabernets in a Bordeaux mould, supple and plummy: the everyday red of the Dordogne, for grilled meat and charcuterie.
Dry Sémillon and Sauvignon, crisp and citrus, for shellfish, river fish and goat's cheese.
An IGP white of Colombard, Ugni Blanc and Gros Manseng: light and crisp, with grapefruit and passion fruit, an inexpensive glass for salads and seafood.
Mauzac sparkling wine, often by the ancestral method, bottled during its one fermentation: green apple and pear, sometimes softly sweet.

made.viticulture: Most vines are trained on wires and pruned to Guyot or cordon, with machine harvesting common in the gentler Bordeaux-style vineyards of Bergerac and Gascony. In Cahors and Madiran the work is about tannin: growers lower yields, open the canopy and wait for ripe skins and seeds, since unripe Malbec and Tannat turn hard and green. Sweet Jurançon is made by leaving Petit and Gros Manseng on the vine into November and December, shrivelling in the dry autumn wind, a process called passerillage; the grapes are picked by hand in several passes, and noble rot is not the aim. Monbazillac is the reverse: the Dordogne's autumn mists bring noble rot to its slopes, and the botrytised berries are picked by hand in successive passes. Spring frost and hail threaten every inland vineyard, as the frost of February 1956 showed when it killed much of the Cahors vineyard, which was replanted with Malbec on grafted rootstocks.
made.winemaking: Red winemaking here is the taming of tannin. Cahors and Madiran see long macerations and often time in oak, though lighter, fruit-led versions exist. Micro-oxygenation, the slow feeding of tiny, measured doses of oxygen into wine in tank, was developed in Madiran in the early 1990s to soften Tannat and fix its colour, and is now used far beyond it. Bergerac, Buzet and Duras blend Merlot and the Cabernets as Bordeaux does. Dry whites such as Jurançon Sec, Bergerac Sec and Côtes de Gascogne are fermented cool in steel to keep fruit and acidity, some on lees or in barrel. Sweet Jurançon ferments slowly from concentrated must and is often aged in barrel; its sweetness is natural, never fortified. Monbazillac is fermented from botrytised must and stopped with sugar left, as in Sauternes. Gaillac keeps the ancestral method for Mauzac, one fermentation finished in bottle, beside the traditional method. Gascony's white grapes also make Armagnac, and Floc de Gascogne blends young Armagnac with grape must.

law.classification: The South West holds a long roll of small AOCs, each with its own grape rules, beneath broad IGPs, Comté Tolosan and Côtes de Gascogne chief among them. The exam's five lead it: Bergerac (1936), with its sweet neighbour Monbazillac (1936); Cahors (1971), red only and at least 70 per cent Malbec; Madiran (1948), red only and led by Tannat; and Jurançon (1936), white only, sold as Jurançon Sec when dry and plain Jurançon when sweet. Around them sit the Bordeaux neighbours on the Garonne and Dordogne (Côtes de Duras, Buzet, Côtes du Marmandais), the Toulouse appellations of Gaillac and Fronton, the Pyrenean ones (Irouléguy, Béarn, Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh) and former VDQS wines raised to AOC in 2011, Saint-Mont and Tursan among them. Bergerac covers every colour, with stricter names inside it for red or sweet wine. Wine made outside the appellation rules is sold under an IGP, and Côtes de Gascogne is the big name there, chiefly for white. Madiran's rules were homologated anew on 26 November 2025, naming Tannat as the main grape.

places.name: Bergerac
places.note: The Dordogne's wine town, south-east of Bordeaux's Right Bank, at the heart of a regional AOC for every colour from Bordeaux's grapes, with stricter names inside it.

places.name: Monbazillac
places.note: Clay-limestone slopes on the south bank facing the town across the river, where autumn mists bring noble rot to Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle for sweet wine.

places.name: Pécharmant
places.note: A red-only appellation on sandy, gravelly hills just north-east of the town, firmer and longer lived than Bergerac red.

places.name: Saussignac
places.note: Sweet whites from botrytised and late-picked grapes on the south bank, west of Monbazillac.

places.name: Montravel
places.note: The western end of the vineyard beside Castillon: dry white and red as Montravel, sweet white as Côtes de Montravel and Haut-Montravel.

places.name: Côtes de Duras, Buzet and Côtes du Marmandais
places.note: Bordeaux's neighbours on the Dropt and the Garonne, making Bordeaux-style reds, rosés and whites from Merlot, the Cabernets and Sauvignon; the Marmandais adds the local Abouriou.

places.name: Cahors
places.note: The Lot valley's red appellation around the town of Cahors: Malbec on the river's gravel terraces, giving rounder wines, and on the limestone causse above, giving firmer, longer-lived ones.

places.name: Gaillac
places.note: An old vineyard on both banks of the Tarn north-east of Toulouse, making every style: Mauzac and Len de l'El for dry, sweet and sparkling whites, Duras, Braucol and Syrah for reds.

places.name: Fronton
places.note: Red and rosé on the Tarn's old terraces north of Toulouse, led by the soft, violet-scented Négrette.

places.name: Marcillac
places.note: A red appellation in the Aveyron on red clay and sandstone, almost wholly Fer Servadou, called Mansois here: peppery and fresh, with red berry and iron notes.

places.name: Entraygues-Le Fel, Estaing and Côtes de Millau
places.note: Three small upland appellations of the Aveyron for light, fresh wines of every colour.

places.name: Côtes de Gascogne
places.note: The IGP of the Gers, Armagnac country, where Colombard and Ugni Blanc once grown for brandy now make crisp, inexpensive whites, with Gros Manseng and Sauvignon Blanc.

places.name: Saint-Mont
places.note: Hills above the Adour north-west of Madiran, an AOC since 2011 for red, rosé and white from Tannat, the Mansengs and other local grapes.

places.name: Tursan
places.note: A small AOC since 2011 in the Landes south of the Adour, whose white keeps the rare Baroque grape.

places.name: Madiran
places.note: Hill country north of Pau where the Gers, the Hautes-Pyrénées and the Pyrénées-Atlantiques meet: red only, led by Tannat on clay and pebbly slopes.

places.name: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh
places.note: The same zone's white appellation, dry or sweet, from Petit and Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac.

places.name: Jurançon
places.note: Steep, south-facing slopes in the Pyrenean foothills south and west of Pau, on clay, sandstone and conglomerate: white only, dry as Jurançon Sec and sweet from shrivelled grapes.

places.name: Irouléguy
places.note: The French Basque Country's appellation around Saint-Étienne-de-Baïgorry, on terraced red sandstone near Spain: firm Tannat-led reds and rosés, and whites from the Mansengs and Petit Courbu.

places.name: Béarn
places.note: A small regional appellation for Tannat-led reds and rosés from vineyards near Orthez and within the Madiran and Jurançon zones.

producers.name: Clos Triguedina
producers.why: A Cahors estate founded in 1830, the usual way into the old vin noir tradition.

producers.name: Château du Cèdre
producers.why: A reference for modern Cahors, ripe and oaked Malbec from the terraces and the causse.

producers.name: Château Montus
producers.why: The Madiran estate whose pure Tannat cuvées lifted the appellation's name from the 1980s.

producers.name: Château d'Aydie
producers.why: A second Madiran reference beside Montus, also making a fortified red from Tannat.

producers.name: Domaine Cauhapé
producers.why: A reference estate for Jurançon, dry and sweet, and the classroom proof that its sweetness is passerillage.

producers.name: Clos Uroulat
producers.why: A Jurançon estate dividing its crop between Jurançon Sec and sweet Jurançon.

producers.name: Château Tirecul La Gravière
producers.why: The Monbazillac estate whose botrytised wines showed the appellation can stand beside Sauternes.

producers.name: Château Tour des Gendres
producers.why: A Bergerac estate whose reds and dry whites show that Bergerac differs from Bordeaux by its address more than its grapes.

producers.name: Domaine Arretxea
producers.why: An Irouléguy estate on the Basque terraces, the usual answer for Basque wine on the French side.

producers.name: Domaine Plageoles
producers.why: A Gaillac family estate that keeps the old local grapes: Mauzac, Ondenc, Len de l'El, Braucol and Prunelard.

exam: Place the region as the Court does: south of Bordeaux and north of the Languedoc, against the Pyrenees, landlocked, with the Dordogne and Bergerac as a column of their own.
Tie each appellation to its grape: Cahors to Malbec (Côt), Madiran to Tannat, Jurançon to Gros and Petit Manseng, Fronton to Négrette, Marcillac to Fer Servadou.
Know Cahors and Madiran as red only, Cahors at least 70 per cent Malbec with Merlot and Tannat beside it.
Separate Jurançon Sec, dry, from Jurançon, sweet from passerillage, grapes shrivelled on the vine, never noble rot.
Know Monbazillac as Bergerac's botrytised sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle, and Bergerac as Bordeaux's grapes on the Dordogne.
Hold the Court's pairings: Cahors and Madiran with duck breast, lamb, foie gras, cassoulet and Périgord truffle; Monbazillac with foie gras, fruit tarts and cheese.
Know micro-oxygenation as Madiran's answer to Tannat's tannin.
Hold the Court's history line: vines grown in the South West since about 125 BC.
traps: Jurançon's sweetness is passerillage, not botrytis; Monbazillac's is botrytis.
Côt and Auxerrois in Cahors are Malbec; the Auxerrois of Alsace is a different, white grape.
Cahors is not Mendoza Malbec: expect earth, iron and firm tannin rather than soft, ripe plum.
Plain Jurançon is the sweet one, off-dry in the Court's outline and gently to richly sweet in the glass; the dry wine says Sec on the label.
Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh is the white of the Madiran zone, not a red.
Bergerac is not Bordeaux: it sits upstream on the Dordogne in its own département with its own AOCs.
Côtes de Gascogne is an IGP, not an AOC.
The Court calls the South West continental, yet the west still takes Atlantic rain and the autumn mists that make Monbazillac.

cards.f: Cahors: the grape, its minimum and its local names
cards.b: Malbec, at least 70 per cent, called Côt or Auxerrois here, with Merlot and Tannat beside it. Red wine only.

cards.f: Madiran: the lead grape and its partners
cards.b: Tannat leads, with Cabernet Franc (Bouchy), Cabernet Sauvignon and Fer (Pinenc). Red wine only; many leading cuvées are pure Tannat.

cards.f: Jurançon Sec against Jurançon
cards.b: Jurançon Sec: dry white, mostly Gros Manseng. Plain Jurançon: sweet (moelleux), Petit Manseng above all, from grapes shrivelled on the vine.

cards.f: Sweet Jurançon: how the sugar is concentrated
cards.b: Passerillage: Petit and Gros Manseng left on the vine into late autumn to shrivel in the warm, dry wind, then picked by hand in several passes. Not noble rot.

cards.f: Monbazillac: the style, the grapes and the cause of sweetness
cards.b: Sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle on the Dordogne's south bank facing Bergerac; noble rot from autumn river mists.

cards.f: Bergerac: where it lies and what it grows
cards.b: On the Dordogne, south-east of Bordeaux's Right Bank: Merlot, the Cabernets and Malbec for red and rosé; Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle for white.

cards.f: The two Manseng grapes of the South West
cards.b: Gros Manseng: larger berries, crisp dry whites such as Jurançon Sec and Côtes de Gascogne. Petit Manseng: small, thick-skinned berries that shrivel on the vine for sweet Jurançon.

cards.f: Micro-oxygenation: where and why it began
cards.b: In Madiran in the early 1990s: tiny, measured doses of oxygen fed into wine in tank to soften Tannat's tannin and fix its colour.

cards.f: Fronton and Marcillac: their grapes
cards.b: Fronton: Négrette, soft and violet-scented, on the Tarn north of Toulouse. Marcillac: Fer Servadou, called Mansois, peppery and fresh, in the Aveyron.

cards.f: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh: what it is
cards.b: The white appellation of the Madiran zone, dry or sweet, from Petit and Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 70 per cent of a Cahors?
questions.exp: Cahors is red only and at least 70 per cent Malbec, called Côt here. Merlot and Tannat may complete the blend, while Négrette belongs to Fronton.

questions.q: By what local name is Malbec known in Cahors?
questions.exp: Cahors calls Malbec Côt or Auxerrois. The Auxerrois of Alsace is a different, white grape, so the name travels badly.

questions.q: Which grape leads the red wines of Madiran?
questions.exp: Madiran is led by Tannat, a deep, tannic grape, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Fer as partners. Malbec leads Cahors and Négrette leads Fronton.

questions.q: Which process concentrates the grapes for sweet Jurançon?
questions.exp: Petit and Gros Manseng are left on the vine to shrivel in the dry autumn wind and picked late in several passes. Noble rot is the route of Monbazillac and Sauternes.

questions.q: Which appellation on the south bank of the Dordogne, facing the town of Bergerac, is known for botrytised sweet white wine?
questions.exp: Monbazillac's slopes catch the river's autumn mists, which bring noble rot to Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle for a sweet wine in the Sauternes mould.

questions.q: Which river flows west from the Massif Central through the Bergerac vineyard?
questions.exp: The Dordogne runs through Bergerac towards Bordeaux's Right Bank. The Garonne gathers the Lot and the Tarn on their way to Bordeaux, the Tarn crosses Gaillac and Fronton, and the Gave de Pau runs down from the Pyrenees past Jurançon.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the wines of Fronton?
questions.exp: Fronton, on the Tarn north of Toulouse, is built on Négrette, soft and violet-scented. Tannat leads Madiran, Fer Servadou Marcillac, and Duras is a Gaillac grape.

questions.q: Which appellation makes the dry and sweet white wines of the Madiran zone?
questions.exp: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh shares Madiran's land and makes white wine only, dry or sweet, from the Mansengs, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac; Madiran itself is red only.

regions.name: Corsica
regions.summary: Corsica is a French island of granite mountains in the Mediterranean, south-east of Provence, north of Sardinia and nearer to Tuscany than to mainland France. Centuries of Genoese rule left it Italian grapes under Corsican names: Nielluccio, genetically Sangiovese, leads Patrimonio on its pocket of limestone; Sciaccarello, pale and peppery, leads Ajaccio on granite; Vermentino makes the whites. Corse, or Vin de Corse, is the island-wide appellation, with five named zones, and Muscat du Cap Corse is a vin doux naturel from the northern peninsula. Rosé is the everyday wine, and the reds and whites carry the island's character.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean: hot, dry summers, mild winters and long hours of sunshine, with most rain falling in autumn and winter and far more of it in the mountains than on the coast. The sea tempers the coastal vineyards, while height brings cooler nights inland. Wind is constant, from the south-westerly libeccio to the mistral and the tramontane from the north, drying the vines and keeping rot away, though summer drought and fire are real hazards.
terroir.soils: Three grounds divide the island. Granite runs through the west and south, under Ajaccio, Sartène, Figari, Porto-Vecchio and much of the Balagne around Calvi, giving light, well drained sandy soils. Schist forms the north-east, Cap Corse and the hills above the eastern coast. Around Patrimonio, in the Nebbio, lies a pocket of limestone and clay-limestone, the reason its Nielluccio is firmer and deeper. The eastern plain is alluvium, clay and sand.
terroir.topography: A mountain in the sea: a spine of granite peaks above 2,000 metres runs north to south, falling steeply to the west coast in deep gulfs and more gently to the flat eastern plain. Vineyards ring the island close to the coast, on valley slopes, hill terraces and the plain, with few far inland. Cap Corse, the narrow peninsula pointing north towards the Ligurian coast, carries small vineyards on steep schist above the sea.
terroir.water: The Mediterranean surrounds every vineyard and none lies far from it; sea breezes cool the coastal slopes at night. The Golo and the Tavignano cross the eastern plain, the Tavignano reaching the sea at Aléria, the old port of the Greek and Roman settlers.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Called Nielluccio, Niellucciu in Corsican: the lead grape of Patrimonio's firm, cherry and herb scented reds and of many rosés, at home on limestone and clay.

grapes.name: Sciaccarello
grapes.styles: Sciaccarellu in Corsican, the same grape as Tuscany's Mammolo: pale, peppery reds of red berries and herbs from the granite of Ajaccio and Sartène, and fine rosé.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: Vermentinu in Corsican and Rolle in Provence: the island's main white, citrus, fennel and almond with a saline edge, and a share of some rosés.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains: the only grape of the vin doux naturel Muscat du Cap Corse.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Widely planted for rosé and for supple Vin de Corse reds, beside the island grapes, with Cinsault, Carignan, Syrah and Mourvèdre as other partners.

grapes.name: Biancu Gentile
grapes.styles: An old island white saved from near extinction, aromatic and full, now bottled alone or in blends by a growing number of estates.

grapes.name: Minustellu
grapes.styles: A revived island red, the same grape as Spain's Graciano, giving colour and acidity to blends.

grapes.name: Aleatico
grapes.styles: A scented red grape of Cap Corse, used for the sweet red called Rappu outside the appellation rules.

wines.note: Nielluccio from limestone: red and black cherry, dried herbs of the maquis and firm, fine tannin; it keeps several years. Serve it with lamb, wild boar or a cured Corsican sausage.
Vermentino with weight and a saline finish: citrus, white flowers and almond, for grilled fish, shellfish and fresh brocciu cheese.
Sciaccarello from granite: pale, perfumed and peppery, with red berries and herbs and light tannin. Serve it cool with charcuterie, roast poultry or tuna.
Pale, dry and crisp from Sciaccarello, Nielluccio and Grenache: red berries, citrus and herbs; the island's everyday wine for summer food.
Vermentino from the granite of the south or the schist of the north: fresh, citrus and lightly floral, a glass for seafood and salads.
A golden vin doux naturel: orange blossom, apricot, honey and grape, sweet but fresh. Serve it chilled as an aperitif or with fiadone, the island's cheesecake of brocciu.

made.viticulture: Old vines were trained as low bush vines, en gobelet, which shade their bunches and stand up to the wind; newer plantings are mostly on wires. The dry, windy summers keep mildew and rot down, so the challenges are drought, heat and fire, and growers on granite and schist pick early enough to hold acidity. In the 1960s and 1970s the eastern plain was planted with high-yielding vines for bulk wine, largely by settlers arriving from Algeria after 1962, and much of that vineyard was later pulled up. Since then the island has turned to its own grapes: growers and research collections have rescued old varieties such as Biancu Gentile and Minustellu, replanted Nielluccio and Sciaccarello on the slopes, and lowered yields. Picking is often by hand on the steep schist of Cap Corse and the granite slopes of the south.
made.winemaking: Rosé, a large part of the crop, is made pale by direct pressing or a short maceration, fermented cool in steel and bottled young. Nielluccio's firm tannin calls for measured extraction and some time in tank or wood, and Patrimonio reds are made to age a few years. Sciaccarello, thin skinned and pale, is handled gently for perfume rather than colour. Vermentino is fermented cool, often kept on its fine lees for texture, and sometimes rested in large wood. Muscat du Cap Corse is a vin doux naturel: neutral grape spirit is added during fermentation, a step called mutage, which stops the yeast and keeps the grape's natural sugar and aroma. The island's aperitifs, such as Cap Corse quinquina, are aromatised wines of the same Muscat and Vermentino country, flavoured with cinchona bark and citrus.

law.classification: Corsica follows French law, with four wine AOCs and an island IGP. Patrimonio, recognised in 1968, was the first Corsican appellation: red and rosé led by Nielluccio, white from Vermentino. Ajaccio became an appellation of its own in 1984, its red and rosé holding at least 40 per cent Sciaccarello. Corse, also written Vin de Corse, is the island-wide regional appellation in three colours, and five zones may add their names to it: Calvi, Sartène, Figari, Porto-Vecchio and Coteaux du Cap Corse. Muscat du Cap Corse, an AOC since 1993, is the vin doux naturel of the northern peninsula and the Patrimonio communes. Wine outside these rules, often varietal and including the island's international grapes, is sold as IGP Île de Beauté, while Rappu, the sweet red of Cap Corse, stays outside the appellations.

places.name: Patrimonio
places.note: The Nebbio around the Gulf of Saint-Florent, west of Bastia, a pocket of limestone and clay-limestone on an island of granite and schist: Nielluccio reds and rosés and Vermentino whites.

places.name: Ajaccio
places.note: Granite hills around the island's capital on the west coast, an appellation of its own since 1984: pale, peppery Sciaccarello reds and rosés and Vermentino whites.

places.name: Corse or Vin de Corse
places.note: The island-wide appellation for red, rosé and white, from the island grapes with Grenache and other southern partners; five zones may add their names.

places.name: Calvi
places.note: The Balagne in the north-west, granite hills between the mountains and the sea, for wines of all three colours.

places.name: Sartène
places.note: Granite valleys in the south-west around the town of Sartène, home ground of Sciaccarello.

places.name: Figari
places.note: A windswept granite plateau in the far south, between Sartène and Bonifacio.

places.name: Porto-Vecchio
places.note: Granite slopes on the south-east coast behind the gulf, for Vermentino whites and Sciaccarello and Nielluccio reds.

places.name: Coteaux du Cap Corse
places.note: Schist slopes on the northern peninsula, for dry Vermentino whites and a few reds and rosés.

places.name: Muscat du Cap Corse
places.note: The vin doux naturel of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains from the schist of Cap Corse and the Patrimonio communes, an appellation since 1993.

places.name: The eastern plain
places.note: The flat alluvial coast south of Bastia around Aléria, which Greek settlers from Phocaea founded in the sixth century BC: the island's volume vineyard, mostly Vin de Corse and IGP Île de Beauté.

exam: Name the island's grapes and their other identities: Nielluccio is Sangiovese and Vermentino is Rolle in Provence; Sciaccarello as Tuscany's Mammolo is asked from Premier Cru.
Tie Patrimonio to Nielluccio on limestone and Ajaccio to Sciaccarello on granite.
Know Patrimonio as the first Corsican AOC, of 1968.
Know Muscat du Cap Corse as a vin doux naturel of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.
Know Corse or Vin de Corse as the regional AOC; its five named zones, Calvi, Sartène, Figari, Porto-Vecchio and Coteaux du Cap Corse, are asked from Premier Cru.
Explain the Italian grapes by history: Genoa ruled the island for centuries before it passed to France in 1768.
Place the island: south-east of Provence, north of Sardinia, granite in the west and south, schist in the north-east.
traps: Nielluccio is Sangiovese, not Nebbiolo, whatever the sound of the name.
Patrimonio's limestone is the exception on an island of granite and schist.
Sciaccarello is pale, but it is made and sold as a red as well as a rosé.
Muscat du Cap Corse is a vin doux naturel, stopped with spirit, not a late harvest wine.
Corsica is French: its wines carry AOC and IGP, never DOC, despite the Italian grapes.
Ajaccio is an appellation of its own, not a named zone of Vin de Corse.

questions.q: Which grape is genetically identical to Corsica's Nielluccio?
questions.exp: Nielluccio is Sangiovese, brought from Tuscany during the centuries of Genoese rule. Nebbiolo is a different Piedmontese grape despite the similar sound.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the wines of Ajaccio?
questions.exp: Ajaccio's red and rosé hold at least 40 per cent Sciaccarello, pale and peppery from granite. Nielluccio leads Patrimonio, Grenache is a southern partner, and Cabernet Sauvignon is grown for IGP Île de Beauté.

questions.q: Which Corsican appellation was recognised in 1968 as the island's first AOC?
questions.exp: Patrimonio, in the Nebbio west of Bastia, became Corsica's first appellation in 1968, for Nielluccio reds and rosés and Vermentino whites.

questions.q: Which soil sets Patrimonio apart from the granite and schist of most Corsican vineyards?
questions.exp: Patrimonio sits on a pocket of limestone and clay-limestone, which gives its Nielluccio a firmer, deeper build than the granite reds of the south.

questions.q: Which grape variety makes the vin doux naturel Muscat du Cap Corse?
questions.exp: Muscat du Cap Corse is made only from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, its fermentation stopped with grape spirit to keep the grape's sugar and aroma.

questions.q: Which grape is the main white variety of Corsica?
questions.exp: Vermentino, Vermentinu in Corsican, makes most of the island's white wine. Biancu Gentile is a revived rarity, Ugni Blanc a minor partner, and Muscat goes into the sweet Muscat du Cap Corse.

questions.q: Which named zone of Vin de Corse lies on a windswept granite plateau near Bonifacio, in the far south?
questions.exp: Figari is the windswept granite plateau of the far south. Calvi lies in the north-west Balagne, Sartène in the south-west valleys, and Coteaux du Cap Corse on the northern schist.

questions.q: Which Tuscan grape is the same variety as Corsica's Sciaccarello?
questions.exp: DNA profiling has shown Sciaccarello to be Mammolo, a minor red grape of Tuscany, just as Nielluccio is Sangiovese.
